admins.accessIntro: How far this admin reaches, and which pages they may open. Off everywhere, they see only their own tree.
admins.bulk.addServersHint: Added to the servers each reseller already has.
admins.bulk.disableBody: These resellers are signed out and cannot sign in, and every customer they hold goes off at once. Switching them back on restores exactly what was running.
admins.bulk.extendHint: Added to each running term. A term that has ended starts again from today; a term on hold gets the days added to the hold. A reseller with no end date is left without one.
admins.bulk.removeServersHint: Taken from each reseller. Their customers already on these servers keep working; they cannot put anyone new there.
admins.bulk.resetBody: Each reseller's traffic allowance starts again from zero, and a reseller paused for using it up is back at once. Their customers' own usage is not touched.
admins.canViewAllClientsHint: Off, this admin sees only their own customers and those of the resellers they created. On, they see every customer on the panel.
admins.canViewAllInterfacesHint: Off, this admin sells only the servers you chose above. On, they may put customers on any server.
admins.enabledHint: Switching this off stops every customer they hold, at once. Their customers' own switches are left alone, so switching it back on restores exactly what was running.
admins.groupHint: What their customers are filed under on your own customer list, so you can see whose they are. They never see it.
admins.lede: Who else signs in to this panel, and how much of it they get.
admins.limitHint: How many users they may sell in all. A customer counts for the users their plan is for: 100 is a hundred one-user customers, or twenty-five for four users each. Empty is no limit.
admins.noGroupsYet: Type a name; a new group is made for it.
admins.noServersGiven: You have not been given a server to sell yet. Ask the panel owner.
admins.noServersWarn: No server chosen: they will not be able to sell anything.
admins.none: No resellers yet. Add one to sell this panel on.
admins.noneAdmins: No admins yet. Add one to manage resellers and customers under them.
admins.onHoldHint: The term starts the first time they sign in, not today: sold on Friday and first signed in on Monday, they still get every day.
admins.page.clients.desc: The customers list and everything done on it.
admins.page.groups.desc: Grouping customers and setting group limits.
admins.page.resellers.desc: Creating and managing their own resellers.
admins.pagesHint: The pages this admin may open. An unchecked page is hidden from them and refused in the backend. Settings, routing, the engine and the admins page are never an admin's.
admins.passwordHint: At least 8 characters. Drawn for you; the copy button beside it puts the address, the username and the password on the clipboard together.
admins.passwordHintEdit: Leave empty to keep the current one. A new password signs them out everywhere.
admins.quotaHint: What all their customers may carry between them. When it is used up every one of them stops, until you start it again.
admins.removeAsk: {name} is about to be removed. What should happen to their customers?
admins.removeAskMany: {name} are about to be removed. What should happen to their customers?
admins.resetConfirm: Start {name}'s traffic allowance again from zero?
admins.role.adminHint: Their own resellers and customers, within the ceiling below. No reach into servers, routing or settings, and no sight of other admins.
admins.role.resellerHint: Only the customers they create, on the servers you choose, within the ceiling below.
admins.serversHint: The servers this reseller may sell. Their own customer form offers exactly these: nothing more, and nothing missing.
admins.sort.name: Name
admins.untilHint: The last day their account works. Empty means it never ends.
admins.you.barred: Your account is paused: {reason}. Your customers are off until it is renewed; ask the panel owner.
admins.you.title: Your account

client.adjust: Set traffic limit and reset cycle
client.attachHint: The selected customers keep every server they already have and gain these as well.
client.baleIdHint: Numeric Bale user ID (0 = none). With the Bale bot on, this user can ask it for their links and usage.
client.batchCountHint: How many clients to create in one go, 1 to 200. Each gets its own keys, files and subscription link.
client.batchMethodHint: How the clients are named: a random handle, your prefix with a running number, or your prefix, a random handle and a postfix.
client.batchPrefixRequired: A prefix is required for this naming
client.bulkResetBody: The usage of every selected customer goes back to zero, and a customer stopped for running out of traffic is back at once.
client.bulkRotateBody: Every selected customer is given new keys and a new subscription link. The files and links they hold now stop working within seconds; each has to fetch new ones.
client.confirmDelete: Delete this client and all its devices?
client.confirmDeleteMany: Delete every selected client and all their devices?
client.confirmPurge: Delete these clients and all their devices?
client.confirmPurgeExhaustedTitle: Delete every customer who has run out of data?
client.confirmPurgeExpiredTitle: Delete every customer whose time has run out?
client.confirmResetAll: Zero the usage of every client on this server?
client.confirmResetAllTitle: Set every customer's usage to zero?
client.connectionsNow: {n} connected now of {limit} users ({files} files issued)
client.consequenceConfigs: Every configuration they hold stops working immediately. Reissuing does not revive the old one.
client.consequenceReset: Customers who had run out become active again.
client.credsNoOpenVPN: None of the tunnels picked signs in with a username and password. WireGuard devices log in with keys the panel generates for each device; nothing to set here.
client.detachHint: These servers are taken away. A customer who would be left with none is refused and named.
client.deviceFilesHint: Every device's configuration, per server and per host, with copy, download and QR: the info button on the customer's row.
client.deviceLimitHint: How many people this plan is for. Each user gets a file of their own, and each file works on one device at a time: a second device on the same file is held off for two minutes. Raising the number issues more files; lowering it removes the newest. Empty = one file, no limit on devices.
client.deviceNamesHint: One credential per name, on every selected server. Empty issues one device called device-1. More can be added later on the customer's page.
client.devicesOnPage: One file per user, named after the customer. Extra files can still be issued and removed on the customer's own page — click their name in the list — where each file has its configuration and QR code.
client.durationHint: Days the plan runs once the customer first connects. Until then it sits on hold.
client.durationRequired: A plan on hold needs a number of days.
client.expiresHint: How long the plan runs from now. Empty or 0 = never expires, on an edit too. Saving a value restarts the countdown from now.
client.expiryResetHint: Counted from now, so saving restarts the countdown.
client.groupHint: Labels to bucket customers by — a reseller, a region, a plan. A customer can be in several. Pick from the ones that exist or type a new name to start one; the groups page and the filter work on them.
client.importHint: The list carries plans, not keys: every customer it makes is issued new files, on the interface chosen above. Choose the file Export clients downloaded, or paste its text.
client.importRename: Import beside it, with a number added to the name
client.importReplace: Replace that customer's plan, keeping their files
client.importSkip: Skip it: the customer here stays as they are
client.l2tpHint: Each user signs in as themselves: one username and password per user, typed into the device's own VPN settings (with the tunnel's pre-shared key for L2TP). The same login is used on every OpenVPN, L2TP, IKEv2, OpenConnect and PPTP tunnel this customer is on. Left empty for a new user, they are generated. Usernames are unique per tunnel; an L2TP password is 6 to 64 characters with no spaces, quotes, # or backslash.
client.linksAfterCreate: Links appear here once the customer is created.
client.linksLead: Where the customer gets their files: the subscription link that serves every device, and the files themselves.
client.menu.delDepletedBody: Everyone out of traffic or out of time is removed.
client.menu.delOrphansBody: Everyone on no server at all is removed.
client.name: Name
client.noGroupsYet: No groups yet — type a name and this customer starts one; it is offered here from then on.
client.noLinks: No shareable links — attach this client to an interface first.
client.noneHint: Add your first customer and hand them their configuration.
client.noneNoInterface: There is nowhere to put a customer yet.
client.noneNoInterfaceHint: A customer lives on a tunnel. Create one first, then come back.
client.notePlaceholder: Contact, plan, anything you need to remember
client.openPage: Open this customer's page: their files one by one, with configurations and QR codes
client.openvpnHint: Each user logs in to OpenVPN as themselves: one username and password per user, on every OpenVPN tunnel this customer is on, carried inside their file. Issued with the file; shown here as they are, so they can be read off or typed over to change them. Left empty for a new user, they are generated. Usernames are unique per tunnel.
client.openvpnPasswordHint: 6 to 64 characters, no spaces. Left empty a password is generated; on an existing customer, left empty it stays as it is.
client.pausedComesBack: Their own switch is on: they come back when the reseller does.
client.pausedStaysOff: Their own switch is off: they stay off when the reseller is back.
client.quotaHint: Data quota for this customer, across every server they use. Empty or 0 = unlimited, on an edit too.
client.rateHint: Download speed cap for this customer, in Mbit/s. 0 = uncapped.
client.resellerPausedHint: Off because the reseller who sold this plan is paused.
client.rotateAllConfirm: Issue {name} a fresh link and fresh keys? Every configuration they hold stops working within seconds, their subscription link changes, and they need the new one. Their address, usage and plan are kept.
client.rotateAllHint: Rotates the subscription link, every WireGuard key pair and preshared key, and every OpenVPN password. Nothing handed out before keeps working.
client.rotateKeysConfirm: Issue {name} fresh keys? Every configuration they hold stops working within seconds, and they need the new files. Their address, usage and plan are kept.
client.rotateKeysHint: Issues a new WireGuard key pair and preshared key, and a new OpenVPN password, for every file this customer holds. What was copied or shared before stops working; rotating the subscription link alone does not do this.
client.rotateOneConfirm: Issue user {n} a fresh {kind} file? The one they hold stops working within seconds.
client.rotateOneHint: Issues one user fresh credentials for one kind of file, and only that: their other files, the other users and the subscription link are untouched. What that file held stops working within seconds.
client.sel.allFilteredSelected: All {n} customers that match are selected.
client.sel.page: All {n} customers on this page are selected.
client.serversHint: One plan across all of them — when one server is blocked, the rest keep working on the same allowance.
client.sort.label: Sort
client.startOnFirstUseHint: Start After First Use: the plan sits unused until the customer first connects, then runs for the plan length. A config handed out on Monday does not burn its month sitting in an inbox.
client.subDisabled: Subscriptions are switched off under Settings.
client.subIdChangeHint: Saving with a different id makes the old link stop working; hand the customer the new one.
client.subIdHint: The secret in the customer's subscription link. Type one to keep a link a customer already has; changing it makes the old link stop working. Letters, digits, - and _, 8 to 64 characters.
client.subRotated: A new subscription link was issued; the old one no longer works.
client.subscriptionIdHint: The secret in the customer's subscription link. Regenerating it invalidates the old link; hand them the new one.
client.subtitle: Each client is one customer. Quota and expiry apply across all their devices.
client.telegramIdHint: Numeric Telegram user ID (0 = none). With the bot on, this user can ask it for their links and usage.
configs.copyRefused: The browser refused clipboard access on an insecure connection.
configs.engine.enforcement.on: Usage is counted and limits are applied in the kernel.
configs.engine.routing.on: Traffic is marked and steered to its outbound.
configs.engine.shaping.on: Rate limits are applied per customer.
configs.lede: What this panel is asking the machine to do, as text.
configs.readOnly: Read-only. The panel rewrites these from the database on every tick.
device.configHidden: The file carries this device's private key. Hand it over with the QR code or the download button; there is no need to read it, and no need for it to be on screen while somebody else is looking.
device.confirmRemove: Remove this device? Its config will stop working.
device.confirmRemoveBody: The customer keeps their other devices.
device.consequenceAddress: Its tunnel address returns to the pool and may be reused.
device.consequenceConfig: The configuration on this device stops working immediately.
device.downloadAllHint: Every device in one zip, one file each
device.name: Device
device.qrHint: Scan this in the WireGuard app to import the tunnel.
device.sharingSuspected: This config appears to be in use on more than one device.
device.title: Devices
enforcement.unavailable: Quota enforcement is not active. Limits are recorded but not applied.
eng.accessLogDesc: Record every request to the panel's API. Off, only errors are logged.
eng.balancer.fallbackInfo: The fallback carries the traffic while no member is up. It has to be a hop of its own; a balancer cannot fall back to another balancer.
eng.balancer.leastPingHelp: Every connection goes to the member that answered the last check fastest.
eng.balancer.noHops: A balancer spreads traffic over hops, and there are none yet.
eng.balancer.randomHelp: Each connection goes to one of the members that is up, and stays with it; the load is spread evenly.
eng.collectIntervalDesc: How often traffic counters are read and limits enforced. 0 keeps the value from the environment. Applies at the next restart.
eng.connectionLimitsDesc: How the outbounds behind balancers are measured. Leave a field at its default unless the checks themselves cause trouble.
eng.deleteBalancerBody: Rules pointing at this balancer have to be changed first; the panel refuses to delete one they still use.
eng.dns.dnsLeakWarning: DNS can leak through the device's old resolver, plain UDP/TCP, or fallback queries. Use DoH upstreams, hosts pins, and skip fallback when privacy matters.
eng.dns.enableDesc: Run a resolver on every tunnel's gateway address and hand it to customers in their profiles, so their lookups never leave the tunnel.
eng.dns.hostsValues: IP address — type and press Enter
eng.dns.listeningDesc: The tunnel addresses the resolver is bound to right now. Empty until saved with at least one server; a profile issued while this is on names its tunnel's gateway as DNS.
eng.dns.serveExpiredTTLDesc: Validity (seconds) of stale cache entries served while a fresh answer is fetched; 0 = never serve stale
eng.dns.strategyDesc: Overall strategy to resolve domain names
eng.enableConcurrencyDesc: Probe all watched outbounds at once instead of one-by-one. Faster, but more visible on the network.
eng.generalConfigsDesc: These options will determine general adjustments.
eng.infoDesc: Every change made here needs to be saved. The collection interval and the log format apply at the next restart; everything else at once.
eng.logConfigsDesc: Logs may affect your server's efficiency. It is recommended to enable them wisely only when needed.
eng.logFormatDesc: Plain text, or one JSON object per line for a log collector. Applies at the next restart.
eng.logLevelDesc: The lowest level written to the log. Applies at once.
eng.maskAddressDesc: IP address mask, when enabled, will automatically replace the IP address that appears in the log.
eng.observatoryAutoManaged: Observers are managed automatically from your balancers. Tune how they probe below — the watched outbounds follow your balancer selectors.
eng.observatoryEmptyHint: No connection observer is active. One runs automatically once you create a balancer, so it can check outbound health before choosing a target.
eng.onlineWindowDesc: How long after its last handshake a device still counts as online.
eng.outboundTestUrlDesc: URL used when testing outbound connectivity. Only Cloudflare's trace reports the exit address and country; any other URL measures latency alone.
eng.probeIntervalDesc: How often each balancer member is measured, in seconds.
eng.probeURLDesc: URL fetched to measure each outbound. The same as the outbound test URL.
eng.resetBody: Every setting on the engine pages goes back to what a fresh install has, including the DNS servers and hosts. Outbounds, balancers and rules are not touched.
eng.routingStrategyDesc: Which address families the names in routing lists resolve to: both, IPv4 only, or IPv6 only.
eng.statsOutboundDesc: Keep a byte counter per outbound in the kernel, for the Traffic column on the outbounds page.
eng.subjectSelectorDesc: Outbound tags this observer probes. Managed automatically from your balancers.
eng.templateDesc: The whole panel configuration as one document. Edit and save to apply; rows are matched by name or tag, and nothing is deleted.

error.noSuchPage: There is no page at that address
error.pageBroke: This page could not be displayed
error.poolFull: This interface has no addresses left. Use a larger subnet or free unused devices.

form.leaveBlankToKeep: Leave blank to keep the stored one
group.addHint: A group can exist before anyone is in it. Assign customers to it afterwards.
group.confirmDelete: Delete the group "{name}"? Its customers are kept and simply ungrouped.
group.confirmDeleteBody: The group is removed. The customers in it are not.
group.confirmDeleteClients: Delete every client in this group, with all their devices?
group.confirmDeleteClientsBody: This deletes the people, not just the label. It cannot be undone.
group.confirmDeleteClientsTitle: Delete every customer in this group?
group.confirmDissolve: Remove this label from its clients? The clients themselves are kept.
group.confirmDissolveBody: Everyone is taken out of it and the group is emptied.
group.consequenceKept.one: {n} customer is kept and simply ungrouped.
group.consequenceKept.other: {n} customers are kept and simply ungrouped.
group.extendHint: Added to each customer's own end date, so anyone with time left keeps it. Anyone already past their date is counted from today and is back on. Customers with no end date are left alone.
group.howTo: Add a group here, or type a name into a client's Group field and it appears. An empty group stays until you delete it.
group.name: Group
group.noneHint: Create one now and assign customers to it, or type a name into a customer's Group field.
group.quotaHint: Replaces the allowance for every member. Leave empty for unlimited.
group.renameHint: Renaming onto an existing group merges the two.
group.subtitle: A group is a label on a client. Use one to act on a batch of customers at once.
history.hint: What this server has been doing, from the last few minutes out to a week.
history.resolution: Exact for the last hour, averaged beyond it.
history.title: History
host.addressHint: The hostname or address a customer's client will dial.
host.emptyHint: Each interface currently hands out its own endpoint. Add a host to offer another address.
host.lede: The addresses customers are handed for each interface.
host.name: Name
host.nameHint: For your own reference; customers never see it.
host.noInterfaces: There are no interfaces yet, so there is nothing to give an address to.
host.portHint: Leave at zero to use the interface's own port
host.priorityHint: Higher wins when several hosts are enabled.
host.removeBody: New configurations will use the next host, or the interface's own endpoint.
host.usingDefault: No hosts configured; using the interface's own endpoint
hosts.checkNow: Check now: try each address the way a customer's device would
hosts.hints.address: Leave blank to inherit the interface's own address.
hosts.hints.excludeFormats: A host left out of a format is not handed out in it: conf is the subscription's plain text, base64 its encoded form, zip the archive, page the browser page.
hosts.hints.remark: A plain label for this host. It names the config a customer is handed for it.
hosts.hints.serverDescription: Optional note shown under the remark.
hosts.hints.shuffle: Hand this host's addresses out in a random order each time.
hosts.hints.tags: Not visible to end users. Letters, digits, _ and : only.
iface.importHint: Paste what Export Interface or Export All Interfaces gave, or choose its file. Each tunnel is made with keys of its own; customers are not part of it. One that cannot be made here, a name or port already taken, is named and the rest are still made.
interface.awgAutoNote: The panel fills every value, fitted to this server. Pick a strength above.
interface.awgClientsNote: Identifier ranges and I1–I5 need AmneziaWG 1.5 or later on the device: the current AmneziaWG and AmneziaVPN apps.
interface.awgDowngraded: This server is too old for AmneziaWG 3, so AmneziaWG 2 was drawn instead.
interface.awgDrawing: Drawing the obfuscation values for this server…
interface.awgEditWarn: Every customer on this tunnel needs their file again after a change here: an old file no longer connects.
interface.awgHint: S1–S4 must be identical on the server and every client of this interface.
interface.awgHint.h: The value each message type is marked with, above 4. A range (from – to) marks each packet with a value of its own from it (AmneziaWG 2.0); the four must not overlap.
interface.awgHint.hpk: AmneziaWG 3 header protection: a key in base64, as a WireGuard key. Needs S1 to S4 of at least 12, and AmneziaWG 3 on every device.
interface.awgHint.i: Packets sent before each handshake to look like another protocol: tags <b 0x…> bytes, <r N> random bytes, <rc N> letters, <rd N> digits, <t> the time. Pick a ready one or write your own.
interface.awgHint.jc: Junk packets sent before each handshake, 0 to 128. Only the sender uses it.
interface.awgHint.jmax: Largest junk packet, in bytes, up to 1280.
interface.awgHint.jmin: Smallest junk packet, in bytes. Smaller than Jmax.
interface.awgHint.s1: Padding on the handshake initiation. Must match on server and clients; S2 must not be S1 + 56.
interface.awgHint.s2: Padding on the handshake response. Must match on server and clients.
interface.awgHint.s3: Padding on the cookie reply. Must match on server and clients.
interface.awgHint.s4: Padding on every data packet. Must match, and has to fit the link: at most 1440 minus the MTU.
interface.awgLevelNote.classic: The profile every AmneziaWG app has ever read, for devices that cannot be updated.
interface.awgLevelNote.modern: Identifier ranges and a disguised packet before each handshake. The current AmneziaWG and AmneziaVPN apps read it.
interface.awgLevelSub.classic: Lighter. Every app, and a weak server.
interface.awgLevelSub.modern: Stronger: ranges and a packet per handshake. A capable server.
interface.awgLinkMtu: Fitted to this server: its way out carries {n} bytes, and every packet, padding included, fits whole.
interface.awgManualNote: You set every value yourself. The server still checks each against AmneziaWG’s rules.
interface.clearBody: They keep their other servers and stop being handed this one. Anyone who would be left with no server at all is refused and named. This is what has to happen before a tunnel can be removed.
interface.clearTitle: Take every customer off this tunnel?
interface.clientAllowedIpsSub: What each device routes into the tunnel. Blank sends everything, 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0.
interface.clientMtuSub: The MTU written into client configs, set apart from the interface MTU. Blank inherits the interface MTU.
interface.cloneHint: The same protocol, MTU, DNS and mode. Its own name, port, address range and keys, no customers, and — for AmneziaWG — a fresh obfuscation profile, so one blocking rule cannot take both down.
interface.consequenceKeys: The tunnel's keys are destroyed. Recreating it issues new ones, so no existing configuration will connect.
interface.editHint: Everything here can be changed. A new port, subnet or mode restarts the tunnel and every customer on it needs their configuration again; a new subnet also gives each device a fresh address.
interface.enabledHint: A disabled interface stops serving its clients.
interface.endpointHint: The hostname or IP customers connect to.
interface.fakeSiteHint: A real site’s host:port, such as www.wikipedia.org:443. Whoever is not a device is relayed to it, and its name is the one a device’s hello asks for. Choose a busy site that is normal to reach from your network and is not blocked.
interface.formSubtitle: Configure mesh endpoint and tunnel routing
interface.hookHint: One command per line. %i stands for the interface name. Runs on the server as root; leave blank unless you need it.
interface.ikev2ModeDesc.eap-tls: Android: a certificate of the device's own, inside EAP.
interface.ikev2ModeDesc.mschapv2: Android, iPhone, Mac and Windows: the device's username and password, and the server's certificate installed once.
interface.ikev2ModeDesc.psk: Android, iPhone and Mac: the username as the identity and the password as the key. Nothing to install.
interface.ikev2ModeDesc.rsa: Android, iPhone and Mac: a certificate of the device's own, downloaded from its page.
interface.ikev2Note: Each device gets one address and one sign-in for every way you turn on; a second sign-in ends the first. Certificates are made and renewed by the panel.
interface.ikev2PortHint: The standard is UDP 500 and 4500, and it always stays open: the VPN built into phones and computers has no setting for another port. Another port is for where those are blocked, and only for clients that take one -- the strongSwan app, Linux. An L2TP tunnel on this server shares 500 and 4500.
interface.keepaliveSub: Seconds between keepalive packets, written into each device. Blank uses the default, 25.
interface.l2tpDevicesLead: Each customer sees their own device’s steps on their page.
interface.l2tpPlainHint: For routers and modems whose L2TP client has no IPsec: Irancell TF-i60 and GP-2101, Huawei 4G/5G, TP-Link, D-Link, Tenda, Xiaomi, ASUS, OpenWrt. Phones and computers keep using IPsec either way, and a modem that asks for a tunnel password is given the pre-shared key.
interface.l2tpPlainOffNote: (turn on the switch above to add these)
interface.l2tpPlainShort: For modems and routers with no IPsec, such as the TF-i60, Huawei and TP-Link.
interface.l2tpPlainWarn: These sessions are not encrypted, and their sign-in can be cracked from a recording. Changing this restarts the tunnel.
interface.l2tpPortHint: The standard is UDP 1701 inside IPsec on UDP 500 and 4500, and it always stays open: the clients built into Windows, macOS and iOS have no setting for another port. Another port is for routers without IPsec that take one. A server carries one L2TP tunnel.
interface.lockedHint: Port, subnet, protocol and mode are baked into every config already issued, so they cannot change after creation.
interface.modeHint: AmneziaWG pads and disguises the handshake so it does not match a known WireGuard fingerprint.
interface.name: Interface
interface.nodeLocked: A tunnel cannot be moved between servers: every customer on it would be stranded.
interface.noneYetHint: Create one before adding customers — a client lives on an interface.
interface.ocCamouflageDesc: Answers like an ordinary website unless the address carries the secret; scanners and filters see nothing to block.
interface.ocCamouflageHint: Customers dial the address with "/?secret" on it; their page gives it whole. Needs ocserv 1.2 or later on the server (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13); an older one runs without it and the panel says so.
interface.ocCertOwn: The tunnel's own certificate is on it: in Cisco Secure Client, Block Untrusted Servers has to be off. A domain with a certificate on the panel avoids that.
interface.ocCertPanel: The panel's certificate is on this tunnel: devices trust it as they are.
interface.ocDtlsDesc: Carries traffic over UDP on the same port once signed in, which is faster. Off: everything over TLS on TCP.
interface.ocPanelCertDesc: When the panel has a certificate for the tunnel's address, devices trust it as they are. Otherwise the tunnel's own is used, and Cisco Secure Client has to be told to accept it.
interface.plainCookieHint: The cookie a device’s proof travels in, as a site’s session cookie would. Left empty, one is drawn; it stays the same when the key turns over.
interface.plainFrontPortHint: The port the front serves plain HTTP on; 80 when empty.
interface.plainHostHint: The name devices connect to over plain HTTP. Never a name a drift transport uses: the network reads this one, and a shared name would give the covered one away.
interface.plainOriginHint: Your own site, such as http://127.0.0.1:8080; required here. Every request that is not a device’s goes there as it came, and its answer crosses the network in the clear, so it must be your site’s own.
interface.pollPathHint: The path the front sends to the relay port, POST requests of up to 64 KB, without buffering them; everything else on the site stays as it is. Left empty, one is drawn. Your web server needs it: it shows here once saved.
interface.portNotStandard: Port {port} is redirected to {std}, which stays open too. The VPN built into Windows, iPhone, macOS and Android cannot be given a port: those devices still dial {std}. Only clients with a port setting use {port}.
interface.postDownSub: Commands the server runs when this tunnel is removed, one per line; %i is the interface name. Usually the rules that undo PostUp.
interface.postUpSub: Commands the server runs when this tunnel first comes up, one per line; %i is the interface name. For custom NAT or firewall rules the panel does not manage.
interface.pptpPortHint: The standard is TCP 1723 with its data in GRE beside it, and it always stays open: the clients built into Windows and most routers have no setting for another port. Another port is for clients that take one. A server carries one PPTP tunnel.
interface.pptpWarn: PPTP’s encryption (MS-CHAPv2 with MPPE) has been broken for years: a recording of a session can be read. Offer it only for routers and modems that have nothing else, and prefer WireGuard, OpenVPN or L2TP/IPsec wherever a device has one.
interface.profileDownloaded: Downloaded. Give this one file to every customer on this tunnel; their username and password is what identifies them.
interface.pskAuto: Left empty, a strong key is generated
interface.pskHint: Every device types this in beside its own username and password. Left empty, one is generated. Changing it later means every device needs the new one, and every session on the tunnel ends.
interface.pskLong: Some routers take a key of at most 32 characters (TP-Link Archer AX23 in its VPN Client); a longer one keeps them out.
interface.pskWeak: A key this short is easy to guess. Keep it only because devices already use it; otherwise leave the field empty for a strong one.
interface.resetUsageBody: Every customer with a device here goes back to zero used. A customer who is also on other tunnels has one total, so this clears all of it for them. Anyone cut off for running out of traffic is back at once. Allowances and dates are unchanged.
interface.resetUsageTitle: Reset usage for everyone on this tunnel?
interface.serverConfigHint: Place this on the server. Peer blocks are written by the panel once the kernel driver lands.
interface.shapeGetPoll: get-poll — GET, data in the query, polled
interface.shapeGetStream: get-stream — GET query, answers on one stream
interface.shapePostStream: post-stream — POST body, answers on one stream
interface.shapePutPoll: put-poll — PUT, data in the body, polled
interface.stillHasClients.one: {n} customer is still on {name}. Take everyone off first — row menu → Take All Clients Off — then delete it.
interface.stillHasClients.other: {n} customers are still on {name}. Take everyone off first — row menu → Take All Clients Off — then delete it.
interface.subnetHint: A /16 holds about 65,000 devices and recycles freed addresses.
interface.subtitle: A listening endpoint on this server. Several may run on different ports.
interface.tlsCertOwn: The tunnel's own certificate is served: devices trust it by its pin, which their profile carries. Its key never changes, so the pin holds across renewals.
interface.tlsCertPanel: The panel's certificate is served: devices check it as a browser does.
interface.tlsHostHint: What devices connect to: a domain pointing at this server, or its address. A domain is also the name the certificate carries and the name devices send; with an address they send none.
interface.tlsOriginHint: Your own site, an http:// address such as http://127.0.0.1:8080; required here. The gateway ends TLS itself and hands whoever is not a device to it as they came, so the port answers as your site does.
interface.tlsPanelCertDesc: When the panel has a certificate in date for this name, and the tunnel is on the panel's own server, it is served and devices check it as a browser does. Otherwise the tunnel's own is served, which devices trust by its pin.
interface.tlsProxyProtocolDesc: Opens every connection to your site with a PROXY protocol v2 header naming the visitor, so its logs show who came. Only for a site set to expect one: any other reads it as a broken request.
interface.transportAnchor: Anchor — WebSocket over TLS, the server itself
interface.transportAnchorHint: Plain WireGuard stays on the tunnel’s port for stock apps. Beside it, a gateway on a port of its own is the web server: it ends TLS with a certificate of its own and takes the same tunnel as WebSocket, with no web server or CDN in front. Whoever does not prove a device’s secret is handed, byte for byte, to your own site, so a probe sees the site and nothing else. Devices trust the certificate by its pin, so no domain is needed. For W-UI’s own app, which reads the profile at ?format=wui.
interface.transportBare: Bare — WebSocket over plain HTTP, the last resort
interface.transportBareHint: For a network where TLS itself gets a connection cut. Plain WireGuard stays on the tunnel’s port for stock apps; beside it, a gateway takes the same tunnel as WebSocket from your web server over plain HTTP. Every session is still sealed end to end and a stranger only ever sees your site, but the network can read that a request was upgraded to WebSocket, so it is the weakest of the transports: use it where nothing covered gets through. Its key turns over every 7 days. For W-UI’s own app, which reads the profile at ?format=wui.
interface.transportDrift: Drift — WebSocket behind your web server or a CDN
interface.transportDriftHint: Plain WireGuard stays on the tunnel’s port for stock apps. Beside it, a gateway takes the same tunnel as WebSocket from your own web server or a CDN, which ends TLS: to the network it is a visit to your site. A request that does not prove a device’s secret goes to your site as it came, so a probe sees the site and nothing else — for W-UI’s own app, which reads the profile at ?format=wui.
interface.transportMirror: Mirror — a borrowed site’s own TLS
interface.transportMirrorHint: The gateway is the server on its own port and borrows a real site. A device opens with a TLS 1.3 ClientHello whose proof hides in its random bytes; the gateway answers with its own handshake. Anyone else — an ordinary visitor, or a probe — is relayed to the borrowed site byte for byte, so they get the site’s real certificate and page and nothing of the gateway’s. For W-UI’s own app, which reads the profile at ?format=wui.
interface.transportMold: Mold — HTTP in a shape you choose, behind a CDN
interface.transportMoldHint: relay that need not look like relay: you pick the shape of every request — its method, where the data rides, and whether the gateway answers each request or writes one long stream. A request that does not prove a device’s secret goes to your site as it came, so a probe sees the site and nothing else. For W-UI’s own app, which reads the profile at ?format=wui.
interface.transportPortFakeTLSHint: The TCP port the gateway is the server on. Devices reach it here; it is always open to the outside.
interface.transportPortHint: A UDP port of its own, beside the tunnel’s; no other tunnel on the server may hold it.
interface.transportPortPlainHint: The TCP port your web server sends the transport’s path to. With no front elsewhere it listens on 127.0.0.1 alone and stays shut in the firewall.
interface.transportPortPollHint: The TCP port your web server or CDN sends the transport’s path to, as plain HTTP. With no front elsewhere it listens on 127.0.0.1 alone and stays shut in the firewall.
interface.transportPortShapeHint: The TCP port your web server or CDN sends the transport’s path to, as plain HTTP. With no front elsewhere it listens on 127.0.0.1 alone and stays shut in the firewall.
interface.transportPortTlsHint: The TCP port devices connect to, opened in the firewall. 443 looks most like a web server; it must not be one another program holds.
interface.transportPortWsHint: The TCP port your web server or CDN sends the transport’s path to, as plain HTTP. With no front elsewhere it listens on 127.0.0.1 alone and stays shut in the firewall.
interface.transportRelay: Relay — HTTP requests behind a CDN without WebSocket
interface.transportRelayHint: Plain WireGuard stays on the tunnel’s port for stock apps. Beside it, a gateway takes the same tunnel as ordinary POST requests from your own web server or a CDN, for a CDN that will not carry WebSocket: the device asks, the answer carries what waits for it, one request at a time. A request that does not prove a device’s secret goes to your site as it came, body and all, so a probe sees the site and nothing else. Slower than drift; use it where drift does not get through. For W-UI’s own app, which reads the profile at ?format=wui.
interface.transportTcpHint: Slower, but on port 443 it looks like an ordinary HTTPS connection. Every customer needs their configuration again after changing this.
interface.transportUdpHint: The right choice unless UDP is being blocked.
interface.transportVeil: Veil — UDP that looks like nothing
interface.transportVeilHint: Plain WireGuard stays on the tunnel’s port for stock apps. Beside it, a gateway on a port of its own carries the same tunnel in packets that show nothing of WireGuard and answers nobody without a device’s secret — for W-UI’s own app, which reads the profile at ?format=wui.
interface.transportWgUdpHint: Plain WireGuard on the tunnel’s port, for every WireGuard app.
interface.wsClientHeaderHint: The header the front names the visitor in, such as CF-Connecting-IP; X-Forwarded-For when empty.
interface.wsFrontPortHint: The port the front serves HTTPS on; 443 when empty.
interface.wsHostHint: The name devices connect to and TLS names: your web server’s domain, or the domain the CDN serves.
interface.wsOriginHint: Your own site, such as http://127.0.0.1:8080: every request that is not a device’s goes there as it came. Empty, such a request is answered 404 and the front dresses it like its own.
interface.wsPathHint: The path the front sends to the drift port; everything else on the site stays as it is. Left empty, one is drawn. Your web server needs it: it shows here once saved.
interface.wsProxiesHint: Addresses or ranges, besides this machine, that may send the transport and say who the visitor is: a CDN’s ranges, say. Anything else is always a stranger. With none, the port listens on 127.0.0.1 alone.
interface.wsShapeHint: The one form every request takes. get-poll and put-poll answer each request; get-stream and post-stream carry the data on one long stream (SSE). get and put ride the query or the body.
interface.xraySniHint: The site whose handshake Reality borrows; one that is reachable from the customers and serves TLS 1.3, such as www.speedtest.net.

login.welcome: Welcome back. Sign in to keep things
node.addressHint: The other panel's own address, as you would open it in a browser.
node.addressHintXui: The panel's access URL with its secret path, as 3x-ui prints it: https://IP:port/path
node.allowPrivate: Allow an address inside this server's network
node.allowPrivateHint: Off by default. Every request to a node carries a token that is full access to a panel, and an address typed by mistake would post it to whatever is listening there. Turn this on only when the node really is on a private network you control.
node.authorityHint: Paste this into the node's own settings, under the panel that manages it. The node then accepts this panel and no other. Only the public half is shown; the key never leaves here, which is why this is worth more than a token that travels in every request.
node.coefficientHint: What a gigabyte through this server costs a customer. 1 is what it counted; 2 charges double for an expensive server; 0.5 discounts a cheap one.
node.confirmDelete: Remove the node "{name}"? Nothing on that server is changed.
node.consequenceRemote: Nothing on that server changes. Its customers keep working.
node.consequenceToken: Its access token stays valid until you revoke it on that panel.
node.dataLimitHint: What this server's host allows per month, and the day of the month it starts again (1-28, or 0 to only clear it yourself). Leave the allowance empty for an unmetered line. Past it, customers are taken off this server and use the others they were sold.
node.fetchPinHint: Reads whatever that address presents right now, without checking it — so do this from a network you trust, and compare it against the node itself if you can.
node.kindPgHint: Versions 1.0 and later, with a node of its own connected. From 5.2: an API key; before it, an administrator's username and password. Its cores' inbounds become tunnels here; each of your files on one is a user there, in a group this panel keeps for that inbound.
node.kindXuiHint: Versions 2.0 and later. Before 3.0: the panel's username and password. 3.0 to 3.2: an API token, and the username and password too for the outbound (and for links on 3.0). 3.3 and later: an API token. Its inbounds become tunnels here, read every 20 seconds; your customers on them are made its clients.
node.lede: The other servers this panel watches.
node.name: Name
node.noneHint: Add one to watch it from here. A node is another W-UI panel.
node.signInHint: For 3x-ui before 3.0, and 3.0 to 3.2 for the outbound; for a Pasarguard before 5.2: an administrator's sign-in on that panel, without two-factor sign-in.
node.spentHint: This server has carried more than its host allows this period. Customers are off it until the allowance starts again.
node.tlsModeHint: The token below lets this panel read every customer's keys on that node, so who answers matters. Verify is right when the node has a real certificate.
node.tlsMutual: Verify, and prove who this panel is
node.tlsMutualHint: This panel presents a client certificate, so the node can refuse a caller that merely knows the token.
node.tlsPinnedHint: This panel accepts only one certificate from this node, whoever signed it.
node.tlsServerNameHint: Optional. The name this panel gives when it connects. A node reached by bare address gives none, and some networks reset a connection that names nothing; Iran's does, between a server inside and one abroad. With "Accept one certificate only" any common name works, since the pin is what is checked. With "Verify normally" it has to be the name on the node's certificate.
node.tlsSkipWarning: Anyone able to sit between this panel and the node can read and change everything it sends, including the access token. Only defensible on a private link.
node.tokenHint: Issue one on that panel with the button above, then paste it here.
node.tokenHintPg: An API key made on that Pasarguard panel under API keys (5.2 and later).
node.tokenHintXui: An API token made on that 3x-ui panel under Settings, API tokens (3.0 and later).
node.tokenKeep: Leave blank to keep the current one
node.tokenNameHint: So you can tell which token to revoke later.
node.tokenOnce: This is the only time it is shown. It is stored as a hash and cannot be recovered.
node.unreachableHint: This server is not answering. The panel still holds the records; the customers on it are the ones who notice.
nodeImport.along: Brought in with them, because they share a tunnel: {names}
nodeImport.explain: Each user becomes a customer here and keeps its credentials, its links and the subscription it already has there; this panel’s subscription carries the same links, beside whatever else the customer is sold. Its allowance, usage and expiry come with it and are kept here from then on; its own limits there are cleared. A user switched off there by hand stays off here.
nodeImport.none: It has no users of its own. Its inbounds appear here within twenty seconds of adding it; read again then.
nodeImport.title: Bring in its users
nodeImport.wuiExplain: That panel’s own tunnels and customers are made here exactly as they are: the same keys, ports, addresses and passwords, so nothing a customer holds changes and nobody has to be sent a new configuration. Their allowance, usage, expiry and groups come with them, and from then on that panel runs them for this one; its subscription links stop being theirs, and this panel’s are. A tunnel moves with every customer on it, so picking one customer brings in everyone they share a tunnel with.
nodeImport.wuiNone: It has no tunnels or customers of its own left: everything on it is this panel’s already.
outbound.addressHint: Host and port, as in de.example.com:51820
outbound.egressHint: Run an HTTP test to show egress IP and country.
outbound.emptyHint: Every customer currently leaves through this server's own address. Add a hop to give some of them another exit.
outbound.form.pasteHint: Paste a link (vmess://, vless://, trojan://, ss://, wireguard://) or a whole .ovpn / .conf file
outbound.form.tagDuplicate: Tag already used by another outbound
outbound.form.uploadConfHint: A wg-quick file: [Interface] and [Peer]. Fills in everything below.
outbound.hopAddressHint: The address this server holds inside their tunnel.
outbound.hopMtuHint: Lower than a normal tunnel, because this one runs inside another.
outbound.importInvalidJson: Invalid JSON — expected an array or an object with a matching key.
outbound.lede: Where a customer's traffic leaves this server.

outbound.nord.noServers: No servers found for the selected country

outbound.pia.noServers: No servers found for the selected country
outbound.privateKeyHint: Issued by whoever runs the upstream server.

outbound.resetAllContent: Are you sure you want to reset the traffic of all outbounds?
outbound.resetOneContent: Are you sure you want to reset the traffic of this outbound?
outbound.saveHint: Changes here are stored as you make them and applied on the panel's next pass, within seconds. Save applies them now. No restart is needed.
outbound.sub.allowPrivateHint: Permit localhost / LAN / private IPs for this subscription's URL. Off by default for security — enable only for a trusted local source.
outbound.sub.empty: No subscriptions yet. Add one above.
outbound.sub.intervalHint: Default 10 minutes. The background job checks frequently; each subscription only re-fetches when its own interval has passed.
outbound.sub.prependHint: Place this subscription's outbounds before your manual ones, so one can become the default.
outbound.sub.previewEmpty: No outbounds found at this URL.
outbound.sub.restartHint: Outbounds from a subscription are stored when it is fetched and applied on the panel's next pass; Save on the page applies them now.
outbound.sub.title: Outbound Subscriptions
outbound.tagHint: Routing rules refer to the outbound by this name.
outbound.testModeTooltip: TCP: fast dial-only probe. HTTP: full request through the outbound. Real delay: total time including connection setup.
outbound.warp.deleteAccountBody: The device is forgotten here. An outbound made from it keeps working until Cloudflare drops the key.
overview.backupDownloaded: Backup downloaded: {name}. It holds every key on this server: keep it like a password.
overview.backupLineDesc: A fresh archive of everything on this server — the database, every interface's keys and every customer — saved to your device.
overview.importFailed: That archive could not be accepted.
overview.keepAddressesDesc: The archive names the server it was taken on. Leave this on when moving to a new server, so customers keep being sent here. Turn it off to clone one server onto another exactly.
overview.restartAllHint: Reopen every tunnel on this server. Changes no records; customers reconnect within seconds.
overview.restarting: Restarting with the restored data. The page reloads by itself when the panel is back.
overview.restoreLineDesc: Put an archive back, from this server or another. You see what you picked before anything changes.
overview.restoreNotBack: The panel has not come back after three minutes. Check the service: systemctl status wui
overview.restoreWarn: Everything on this panel is replaced with the archive's contents, and the panel restarts. Its customers, keys and accounts come from the archive: afterwards you sign in with the archive's administrator. How this panel is reached — its port, URL path and certificate — stays this server's. What is here now is saved first, so this can be undone from the list of backups.
overview.stopAllBody: Every customer on this server is disconnected and cannot reconnect until the tunnels are turned back on. They stay off across a restart. Nothing is deleted and no allowance changes.
overview.stopAllHint: Switch every tunnel off. Nobody can connect until they are turned back on.
overview.throughputSub: Traffic across every interface on this host
overview.tunnelsHint: How many tunnels on this server are actually carrying traffic, out of how many exist.
overview.uploadCut: The upload was cut off. Check the connection and try again.
routing.balancer.strategy.leastPing: Every connection goes to the member that answered the last check fastest.
routing.balancer.strategy.random: Each connection goes to one member, chosen by hash, so the load spreads evenly and a connection stays put.
routing.blockBitTorrentHint: Covers the default ports. A client moved off them is not caught.

routing.defaultOutboundHint: Traffic that does not match any routing rule uses this outbound.
routing.directNotice: A direct connection ensures that specific traffic is not routed through another server.
routing.domainHint: Resolved every fifteen minutes and matched by address.
routing.failClosed: Block traffic while the default outbound is down

routing.firstMatchWins: Evaluated top to bottom; the first match decides.
routing.inactive: Routing is stored but not applied
routing.ipv4RoutingDesc: These options will route traffic based on a specific destination via IPv4.
routing.noRuleMatched: No routing rule matched — traffic goes to the default outbound:
routing.noRules: No rules yet. Everything follows the default outbound.
routing.portHint: A port or a range, as in 25 or 6881-6889.
routing.removeBalancerBody: Rules pointing at it must be changed first.

routing.rule.name: Name
routing.rule.nameHint: So the list can be read six months from now.
routing.rule.valueHint.client: One customer's traffic, wherever it is going.
routing.rule.valueHint.domain: One or more names. Subdomains are matched by address, not by suffix.
routing.rule.valueHint.ip: Addresses, ranges, or a named group.
routing.rule.valueHint.protocol: Which transport this rule applies to.
routing.saveHint: Basic Routing is stored and applied when you press Save. Rules and balancers are stored when their own form is saved, and applied within seconds. No restart is needed.
routing.splitExclude: Keep these out of the tunnel

routing.splitIncludeDesc: Only the destinations below go through the tunnel; everything else is dropped.
routing.splitListHint: Domains, addresses, ranges, geoip: entries or named groups.

routing.splitOffDesc: The lists below describe the routing on their own.

routing.targetHint: An address, a range, or a named group such as private or bogon.
routing.testerNotice: Ask the router which outbound would handle a connection. No traffic is sent — the decision comes straight from the live routing engine.
routing.tunnels.hint: Everyone on these interfaces leaves through here. Saved as a routing rule; narrower rules above it still come first.

set.baleEventBusNotifyDesc: Which events the Bale bot tells the administrators of

set.baleTokenDesc: The bot's token, from @BotFather in Bale.
set.datepickerDescription: Scheduled tasks will run based on this calendar.

set.defExpiryDesc: How many days a new customer has. 0 is no expiry.

set.externalTrafficInformURIDesc: The http or https address the traffic is posted to.
set.infoDesc: Changes are kept once you press Save. Where the panel and the subscription service listen, their certificates, the trusted proxies and the time zone take effect at the next restart; everything else at once.
set.informBody: Each interval, every customer's new traffic is POSTed as JSON: [{"email","up","down"}].
set.nodes.apiTokenHint: The remote panel exposes its API token under Authentication → API Token.
set.pageSizeDesc: Define page size for the interfaces table. (0 = disable)

set.panelListeningIPDesc: The IP address for the web panel. (leave blank to listen on all IPs)
set.panelOutboundDesc: The outbound the panel's own traffic leaves through: its probes, the bot, other panels.

set.remarkTemplateDesc: When set, this replaces the remark model for every subscription link — write your own format with the variable tokens (use the button to insert them). Leave empty to use the model above.
set.restartConfirm: Restart the panel now? Every open page loses its connection for a few seconds.
set.security.apiTokenCreatedNotice: Copy this token now. For security it is not stored in readable form and will not be shown again.
set.security.apiTokenEmpty: No tokens yet — create one to authenticate bots or remote panels.
set.security.twoFactorEnableDesc: Adds an additional layer of authentication to provide more security.
set.sessionMaxAgeDesc: The duration for which you can stay logged in. (unit: minute)
set.smtpEventBusNotifyDesc: Select which events trigger email notifications

set.smtpFromNameDesc: Optional display name shown before the sender address in the From header.
set.smtpPasswordConfigured: Configured; leave blank to keep current password.
set.smtpPasswordPlaceholder: Configured - enter a new password to replace
set.subAnnounceDesc: The announcement text displayed in the VPN client. Supports client identity tokens: {{EMAIL}}, {{ID}}, {{SHORT_ID}}, {{SUB_ID}}, {{TELEGRAM_ID}}.
set.subCertPathDesc: The certificate the subscription service serves when it listens on a port of its own. Empty uses the panel's own certificate. (begins with '/')

set.subUpdatesDesc: The update intervals of the subscription URL in the client apps. (unit: hour)
set.telegramAPIServerDesc: The Telegram API server to use. Leave blank to use the default server.
set.telegramChatIdDesc: The Telegram Admin Chat ID(s). (comma-separated)(get it here @userinfobot) or (use '/id' command in the bot)
set.telegramNotifyTimeDesc: How often the Telegram bot sends periodic reports. Pick a preset interval, or choose Custom to enter a raw crontab expression.
set.telegramTokenConfigured: Configured; leave blank to keep current token.
set.telegramTokenDesc: The Telegram bot token obtained from '@BotFather'.

set.tgBackupBotOff: The bot is off, so no backup is sent. Turn it on in the Panel Settings tab.
set.tgBackupTimeDesc: In the panel’s time zone ({zone}). A backup that falls due while the panel is off is sent as soon as it is back.
set.tgEventBusNotifyDesc: Select which events trigger Telegram notifications
set.timeZoneDesc: Scheduled tasks will run based on this time zone.
set.trafficDiffDesc: Get notified about traffic cap when reaching this threshold. (unit: GB)
set.trustedProxyCidrsDesc: Comma-separated IPs/CIDRs allowed to set forwarded host, proto, and client IP headers.
set.twoFactorModalDeleteDesc: Enter the code from your app, or your password, to turn it off.

set.twoFactorModalSecondStep: 2. Enter the code from the app
set.twoFactorModalSteps: To set up two-factor authentication, perform a few steps:
settings.apiTokensDesc: Long-lived credentials for machine access — another panel using this one as a node, or a script. A token here can do everything you can, so revoke any you do not recognise. New ones are issued from the Nodes page, where the machine that needs one is.
settings.backupEveryDesc: Zero turns scheduled backups off. The schedule is read from the newest archive on disk, so restarting the panel does not postpone it.
settings.backupKeepDesc: How many archives to keep. Older ones are removed after each backup.
settings.backupPasswordDesc: Every archive taken from now on is encrypted with it, the ones sent to Telegram included. It is kept on this server, never in a backup: write it down somewhere else, or an encrypted archive cannot be restored.
settings.backupPasswordSaved: Backup password saved; archives are encrypted from now on
settings.backupsWarning: An archive holds the database, every interface key and every customer credential. Treat one like a password file.
settings.botTokenDesc: From @BotFather. Stored on this server and never shown again once saved.
settings.changePasswordDesc: The password is stored hashed and cannot be recovered - only replaced.
settings.chatIdDesc: Where messages go. Send your bot a message and read the id from @userinfobot.
settings.confirmPasswordToDisable: Enter your password to turn it off.
settings.dataDirDesc: Where customers, keys and usage are stored.
settings.defDevicesDesc: How many configurations a new customer is issued.
settings.defExpiryDesc: How long a new customer's access lasts. Zero means it never expires.
settings.defQuotaDesc: What a new customer starts with. Zero means unlimited.
settings.defRateDesc: The ceiling a new customer is capped at. Zero means uncapped.
settings.defResetDesc: How often a new customer's allowance is restored.
settings.fillCredentials: Enter the current password and a new username or password.
settings.languageDesc: The language the panel opens in.
settings.languageHint: Saved to your account, so it follows you to another device.
settings.leaveBody: Leaving now discards them. Save first, or discard and go.
settings.lede: How this panel behaves, and what new customers start from.
settings.listenDesc: Where the panel is answering now. A change made on General, or with the w-ui command, takes effect at the next restart.
settings.mailEnabledDesc: A second way for an alert to reach you. Telegram is the one people set up and the one that stops working when a token is revoked or Telegram is blocked on this server's network; mail is slower, duller, and keeps working.
settings.mailEncryptionDesc: How the session with the mail server is protected. If a username is set, the panel refuses to send it unencrypted.
settings.mailFromDesc: Who the message is from. Most providers refuse an address that is not yours.
settings.mailFromNameDesc: The name shown beside the address. Optional.
settings.mailHostDesc: The SMTP server that will accept the message. Your mail provider publishes this.
settings.mailKindsDesc: Its own list, separate from Telegram's. The point of a second channel is that it can carry less — Telegram every time a customer runs out, mail only when the panel itself is in trouble.
settings.mailNoTLS: None — a mail server on this machine
settings.mailPasswordDesc: Stored, never shown again. Use an app password where your provider offers one: this is often an account password, and it does not belong in a panel.
settings.mailPortDesc: 587 for STARTTLS, 465 for TLS, 25 for a mail server on this machine.
settings.mailToDesc: Where alerts go. Several addresses can be separated by commas.
settings.mailUsernameDesc: Leave empty for a server that accepts mail from this machine without signing in.
settings.mtlsTrust: Panel allowed to manage this one
settings.mtlsTrustCleared: Cleared. The token is the only check again.
settings.mtlsTrustHint: Paste the authority from the panel that manages this one. It will then have to present a client certificate as well as its token, so a token read out of a log or a backup is no longer enough. Leave empty to accept the token alone.
settings.mtlsTrustSaved: Saved. The managing panel must now present its certificate.
settings.note: Changes apply immediately. Nothing here restarts the panel.
settings.notifyEnabledDesc: The panel is not watched. Without this, a customer running out at three in the morning is something you hear about from them.
settings.notifyKindsDesc: Choose nothing and everything is sent.
settings.orEnterKey: Or type this key in by hand:
settings.passwordMismatch: The two passwords do not match.
settings.passwordTooShort: The new password must be at least 8 characters.
settings.processConfigDesc: Listening address, data directory, log level and collection interval are set on the server. Run this command over SSH.
settings.quotaEngineOn: The kernel stops a customer at the byte they run out.
settings.recentLogDesc: The last few hundred lines, kept in memory. For the full history use journalctl on the server.
settings.reconcilerDesc: Rebuilds kernel state from the database on every tick.
settings.restoreBody: Everything on this panel is replaced by what was in the archive: customers, keys and accounts — afterwards you sign in with the archive's administrator. How this panel is reached — its port, URL path and certificate — stays this server's. The current state is saved as a backup first, so this can be undone. The panel restarts and the page reloads once it is back on the restored data.
settings.restoreStarted: Restoring. The panel is restarting and this page will reload.
settings.revokeBody: Whatever is using “{n}” stops working immediately, and the token cannot be brought back. A node using it will go unreachable until it is given a new one.
settings.scanThis: Scan this with your authenticator app, then enter the code it shows.
settings.sessionDesc: How long a sign-in lasts before the password is asked for again.
settings.shapingOn: Each limited customer has a queue of their own.
settings.subtitle: This panel and this operator account.
settings.testMailDesc: Sends one message with the saved settings. A wrong password is better found here than on the night the server has a problem.
settings.testNotifyDesc: Sends one message now, so you find out here whether the token works rather than from a missing alert months later.
settings.twoFactorDesc: The panel's password is the only thing between an attacker and every customer's configuration. A second factor makes a leaked password a nuisance instead of a breach.
settings.uploadFailed: That archive could not be accepted.
settings.uploaded: Archive accepted. Restore it when you are ready.

sharing.caveat: This is evidence, not proof. A phone moving between wifi and mobile data changes address on its own, and a mobile carrier can put two unrelated customers behind one address. Nothing here is disconnected automatically. Look at the addresses and decide.
sharing.historyHint: Every device that shows on the list, and every one held off for going over its plan, is kept here: after it leaves the list, and after the customer is deleted.
sharing.import.denied: This server’s log, for the time before records were kept, could not be read: {error}
sharing.import.done: {n} records were read back from this server’s log, for the time before they were kept.
sharing.import.doneNone: This server’s log was read back for the time before records were kept; it held none.
sharing.import.failed: Reading this server’s log back failed: {error}
sharing.import.unavailable: This server has no system log to read the time before records were kept from.
sharing.lede: Credentials reaching the server from several places at once.
sharing.noneHint: No credential has been seen from three or more places inside ten minutes.
sort.name: Name A–Z
sub.disabled: The subscription service is switched off, so this link will not answer.
sub.enabledDesc: Serve each customer their own configuration at a link their app can refetch, so a new device or a moved endpoint reaches them without you sending anything.
sub.hostDesc: Leave blank to use whatever address the panel was reached on. Set it when the panel sits behind something.
sub.intervalDesc: What the customer's app is told about how often to check for changes.
sub.pathDesc: Where the service answers. Choose something of your own: a path anybody could guess is a path somebody will.
sub.proxyDesc: The full address customers reach, when a proxy in front rewrites the path.
sub.rotateBody: Every copy of the current link stops working immediately, including the one on the customer's device.
sub.rotated: A new link has been issued
sub.title: Profile name
sub.titleDesc: What the customer's app shows this subscription as.
update.askNode: Ask this node to update itself
update.askNodeBody: No binary is sent from here. The node fetches the release from the project itself and checks the signature before installing it, then restarts. Its customers stay connected while it does.
update.askNodeTitle: Ask this node to update its own panel?
update.cameBackOld: The panel restarted on the version it had. Check the service: systemctl status wui
update.failed: The update was not installed. The panel keeps running the version it had.
update.installing: Putting the new panel in place…
update.needsHelper: This server runs the panel without permission to replace its own binary, and the helper that does it for the panel is not installed yet. Run this once on the server as root — it installs this release and the helper, and from then on updates install from here:
update.nodeStarted: The node is installing {v} and restarts by itself when it is done.
update.nodeUpdated: The node updated to {v} and is restarting.
update.notBack: The panel has not come back after three minutes. Check the service: systemctl status wui
update.restarting: Restarting on {v}… The page reloads by itself when the panel is back.
update.title: Panel update
update.unsigned: This build carries no release-signing key, so it will not install an update. That is deliberate: a panel that installed an unverified binary would be worse than one that does not update.
update.whatHappens: The panel downloads the release itself, checks it against a signing key built into this binary, replaces itself and restarts. Nothing unsigned is ever written to disk. Customers stay connected: the tunnels are in the kernel and outlive the panel process.
